scenario: 1 · P3 — ZDT2-type, 10 variables, smooth *concave* front, unconstrained, 2 objectives, cheap evaluations
recommended algorithm: **MOEA/D-DE** (best IGD in D.1); NSGA-II as the safe, parameter-light default
why (problem properties): Concave front ⇒ weighted-sum methods can never reach the interior (✔ in the P3 study the weighted sum returned only 2 points, 0 of them with 0.25<f1<0.75, vs 0 for the Tchebycheff-type weight metric (p=∞)); population methods need no convexity. Two objectives ⇒ Pareto ranking still has discriminating power, evaluations are cheap ⇒ a population method with a good variation operator is enough.
runner-up and why it loses: NSGA-II: ✔ rank 7 (IGD 0.0127 ± 0.0151) – a few of 10 seeds get trapped on ZDT2's local front (std > mean). Note also that plain SBX-based MOEA/D ranked 13/13 (IGD 0.1283): the DE operator, not decomposition alone, is what makes MOEA/D-DE win.
evidence: ✔ D.1 table: MOEA/D-DE rank 1, IGD 0.0045 ± 0.0004 over 10 seeds.

scenario: 2 · P5 — beam design: **constrained** (the constraint is active on the front), 2 variables, 2 objectives, curved front
why (problem properties): Only 3 % of random P5 points are infeasible, yet the constraint is *active*: ✔ an NSGA-II that ignores it ends with 45 % infeasible solutions. A penalty method needs a tuned penalty weight (too small → infeasible 'winners', too big → premature convergence at the boundary); constrained domination needs no parameter and always prefers feasible solutions. Honest caveat: with only one mild constraint the measured advantage over penalty-NSGA-II is small.
runner-up and why it loses: NSGA-II with static penalty: ✔ rank 5 vs C-NSGA-II rank 4 on P5 (IGD 0.0112 vs 0.0107 – inside one std, so a tie; MOABC and SMS-EMOA had the lowest IGD).
evidence: ✔ D.1 (P5) head-to-head + infeasible-share numbers; ○ the rest is reasoning.

scenario: 3 · P10 (M = 5) — **many-objective**, spherical front, 14 variables, plenty of evaluations
recommended algorithm: **HypE** (best IGD in D.2); NSGA-III is the default textbook choice
why (problem properties): With M = 5 Pareto dominance stops discriminating (✔ 57 % of a random population is already non-dominated at M=5 vs 35 % at M=3) and crowding distance fails; reference-point/reference-vector designs keep diversity structurally.
runner-up and why it loses: NSGA-II: ✔ IGD 0.6696 vs 0.3229 for the winner (mean of 10 seeds).
evidence: ✔ D.2 ranking: HypE < RVEA < NSGA-III < MOEA/D < NSGA-II

scenario: 4 · P8 — bi-objective TSP-15 (permutations), cheap evaluation, **tight budget** (~1 000 evaluations)
recommended algorithm: **MOACO** at the small budget; MOEA/D-ACO when the budget grows
why (problem properties): Permutation encoding makes SBX/polynomial mutation useless; the problem has heuristic information (1/distance, 1/time) that constructive ACO methods exploit from the first iteration, a decisive advantage when only ~1 000 evaluations are allowed.
runner-up and why it loses: NSGA-II with order crossover/swap: needs the larger budget to catch up (see the D.3 IGD table).

scenario: 5 · P9 — feature selection (30 binary variables, **each evaluation = 5-fold model training**, budget ≈ 3 000)
recommended algorithm: **MOMA** or NSGA-II with bit-flip operators; if evaluation were much more expensive, add a surrogate
why (problem properties): Binary encoding and an expensive objective ⇒ need operators that exploit structure cheaply: bit-flip local search around good subsets (memetic) uses evaluations where they matter. The problem is also *discrete*, so gradient or classical scalarisation (needs a single-objective solver for a binary programme) is unattractive.
runner-up and why it loses: MOGWO (continuous swarm, mapped to binary): works (✔ logged in the implementation table) but its continuous update is not designed for subsets.
evidence: ○ reasoning plus ✔ the P9 runs for algorithms 23 and 30 in the implementation log (A3).

scenario: 6 · P14 — laptop choice where the decision maker already has an **aspiration point (1.8 kg, 12 h)**
why (problem properties): The DM does not need the whole front; concentrating the budget near the aspiration point gives a denser set of relevant trade-offs. Because the aspiration is *dominated* by the true front, R-NSGA-II is expected to converge onto the front region closest to it.
runner-up and why it loses: NSGA-II + a posteriori TOPSIS/VIKOR: works, but spends most of the population on irrelevant regions.
evidence: ✔ the P14 R-NSGA-II run (algorithm 35): front spans 1.69–1.80 kg, whereas the full front spans 1.53–2.13 kg.
